content: The efficacy of multiple direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens approved for adults and those under development cannot be realistically compared through direct trials. Instead, data from adult clinical trials can be extrapolated to define criteria for selecting the most promising regimens for treating children. Approval of these regimens should be based on pre-authorization phase I/II clinical studies involving 30–40 children, focusing on pharmacokinetics, tolerability, and limited efficacy data. Post-licensure studies should then collect long-term and more detailed safety and efficacy data. Palatability and age-appropriate formulations must be prioritized and developed to ensure compliance in pediatric populations. Ongoing studies are investigating the use of DAAs in children and adolescents with chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. These studies include various combined regimens targeting multiple genotypes, with expected completion dates ranging from 2018 to 2022. There is a need for pediatric formulations, such as granules, for children under six years of age. Long-term follow-up studies are required to assess the impact of treatment on growth, cognitive function, and educational attainment. Currently, no long-term studies beyond 24 weeks post-treatment are available for DAAs in children. Future trials should include children whose DAA regimens have failed and ensure genotype coverage reflects that of adult studies. Cost-effectiveness studies are necessary to evaluate the treatment of children with DAAs, including acceptability and quality of life outcomes. Research gaps include understanding the epidemiology, burden, and natural history of chronic HCV infection acquired vertically or in childhood and adolescence. This includes the long-term clinical outcomes of chronic HCV and the extent of undiagnosed pediatric/adolescent HCV infections. Prioritization of DAA regimens for pediatric development should involve extrapolating data from adult clinical trials and applying criteria to select the most promising regimens for children. Additionally, there is a need for interferon-free options for genotypes 2 and 3, as well as potential shortening of treatment regimens to eight weeks. Future studies should identify the best combinations for treating adolescents and children, determine the optimal timing for initiating treatment, and address the management of treatment failures.
